claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ISARIC, 2020 and Langford et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The pandemic may result in a large cohort of COVID-19 survivors with residual post-COVID-19 chronic lung disease (such as interstitial lung disease and bronchiectasis) who will be at risk of acute exacerbations.
claims.source: It is also likely that the pandemic may result in a large cohort of COVID-19 survivors with residual post-COVID-19 chronic lung disease (such as interstitial lung disease and bronchiectasis) who will be at risk of acute exacerbations (George et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to George et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Extensive lung damage has been reported on high-resolution chest computed-tomography several weeks into COVID-19 illness.
claims.source: Long-term sequelae of individuals recovered from moderate to severe COVID-19 is currently unknown, but extensive lung damage has been reported on high-resolution chest computed -tomography several weeks into the illness (Zhao et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2020.

claims.claim: In patients with post-COVID-19 structural lung damage, frequent courses of antibiotics and hospital admissions may lead to increased risk of colonisation and infection with resistant organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
claims.source: In patients with post-COVID-19 structural lung damage, frequent courses of antibiotics and hospital admissions may lead to increased risk of colonisation and infection with resistant organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Rodrigo-Troyano and Sibila, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rodrigo-Troyano and Sibila, 2017.

claims.claim: There is mounting evidence of a lack of efficacy of chloroquine for treating COVID-19.
claims.source: For example, despite mounting evidence of a lack of efficacy (Kashour et al., 2021; UKRI, 2020; WHO, 2020e), the antimalarial drug chloroquine has been used to treat COVID-19.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kashour et al., 2021; UKRI, 2020; WHO, 2020e.

claims.claim: Chloroquine remains the drug of choice for malaria in high non-Plasmodium falciparum prevalence malaria settings.
claims.source: This is of particular concern in high non-Plasmodium falciparum prevalence malaria settings, where chloroquine remains the drug of choice for malaria (WHO, 2015b)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2015b.

claims.claim: COVID-19 symptoms could be mistaken for other diseases such as malaria or tuberculosis (TB), and vice versa.
claims.source: Because a patient with COVID-19 can present with non-specific symptoms (e.g. fever and/or persistent cough), these could be mistaken for other disease such as malaria (Chanda-Kapata et al., 2020) or tuberculosis (TB) (The Lancet Hiv, 2020), and vice versa.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chanda-Kapata et al., 2020 and The Lancet Hiv, 2020.

claims.claim: The widespread use of azithromycin for WHO-recommended mass drug administration campaigns for trachoma has resulted in bystander selection.
claims.source: The importance of such bystander selection has already been seen following the widespread use of azithromycin for WHO-recommended mass drug administration campaigns for trachoma (O'Brien et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to O'Brien et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The initial use of hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and azithromycin for COVID-19 has now been halted in some settings (e.g. in the US).
claims.source: As the evidence mounts on the lack of efficacy of hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and azithromycin for treatment of COVID-19, their initial use has now been halted in some settings (e.g. in the US [Acosta et al., 2020; Bull-Otterson et al., 2020; Kadri et al., 2020]).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Acosta et al., 2020; Bull-Otterson et al., 2020; Kadri et al., 2020.

claims.claim: In many African countries, despite WHO recommendations, hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and azithromycin were still being advised for use in the summer of 2020.
claims.source: For example, in many African countries, despite WHO recommendations, hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and azithromycin were still being advised for use in the summer of 2020 and may be still being used off-label (Abena et al., 2020; Belayneh, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abena et al., 2020 and Belayneh, 2020.

claims.claim: In India, it appears to still be guidance to use hydroxychloroquine as a prophylactic for 'healthcare workers'.
claims.source: In India, it appears to still be guidance to use hydroxychloroquine as a prophylactic for 'healthcare workers' (National Taskforce for COVID-19, India, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to National Taskforce for COVID-19, India, 2020.

claims.claim: Cheap, rapid tests may detect SARS-CoV-2 infections earlier and hence prevent some antibiotic use.
claims.source: In community settings, cheap, rapid tests may detect SARS-CoV-2 infections earlier (Mina et al., 2020), especially in the face of unspecific symptoms, and hence prevent some antibiotic use.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mina et al., 2020 and involves inference about the impact on antibiotic use.

claims.claim: Some current diagnostics for asymptomatic testing in the community, such as lateral flow tests, remain insensitive and risk providing 'false negatives' with a sense of security that is not accurate.
claims.source: Moreover, some current diagnostics for asymptomatic testing in the community, such as lateral flow tests, remain insensitive and risk providing 'false negatives' with a sense of security that is not accurate (Mahase, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mahase, 2020.

claims.claim: Prolonged changes in antimicrobial use in humans during the COVID-19 crisis could mean increased antimicrobial production, which may accelerate changes in antimicrobial concentrations in the environment.
claims.source: If prolonged, changes in antimicrobial use in humans during the COVID-19 crisis could mean increased antimicrobial production, which may accelerate changes in antimicrobial concentrations in the environment and, consequently, affect selective pressures for AMR in water and soil systems (WHO, 2020a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2020a and involves speculation about future impacts.

claims.claim: Disruption within a single Chinese factory resulted in an international shortage of piperacillin-tazobactam.
claims.source: The fragility of the antibiotic pipeline was highlighted recently when disruption within a single Chinese factory resulted in an international shortage of piperacillin-tazobactam (Davis, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis, 2017.

claims.claim: In some countries, such as the UK, 80–90% of generic medicines are imported.
claims.source: In some countries, such as the UK, 80–90% of generic medicines are imported (Business and Energy and Industrial Strategy Committee, 2018)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Business and Energy and Industrial Strategy Committee, 2018.

claims.claim: Most countries are net importers of antibiotics.
claims.source: Indeed, most countries are net importers of antibiotics (Simoes and Hidalgo, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Simoes and Hidalgo, 2011.

claims.claim: Countries that manufacture and export antibiotics are facing increased home market demands due to COVID-19 which may lead to a reduction in exports, as seen in India.
claims.source: Countries that manufacture and export antibiotics are facing increased home market demands due to COVID-19 which may lead to a reduction in exports, as seen in India (Government of India, 2020; Guerin et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Government of India, 2020 and Guerin et al., 2020.

claims.claim: 10 manufacturers have reported shortages of azithromycin to the US Food and Drug Administration, potentially because of its use for COVID-19 treatment.
claims.source: As COVID-19 is also likely to lead to changes in the use of antibiotics, this will have a similar effect on supply chain shortages; 10 manufacturers have reported shortages of azithromycin to the US Food and Drug Administration, potentially because of its use for COVID-19 treatment (US Food and Drug Administration, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to US Food and Drug Administration, 2020.

claims.claim: Low- and middle-income country (LMIC) settings are particularly vulnerable to supply chain issues where weak health systems and poor quality control of medicines are barriers to antimicrobial access.
claims.source: Low- and middle-income country (LMIC) settings are particularly vulnerable to supply chain issues where weak health systems and poor quality control of medicines are barriers to antimicrobial access (Frost et al., 2019; Laxminarayan et al., 2016; Pokharel et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frost et al., 2019; Laxminarayan et al., 2016; Pokharel et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Uneven supplies of different antimicrobials across all income settings raise concerns about AMR emergence due to suboptimal antibiotic use.
claims.source: Uneven supplies of different antimicrobials across all income settings (Pauwels et al., 2015; Tickell et al., 2019) raise concerns about AMR emergence due to suboptimal antibiotic use (Access to Medicine Foundation, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pauwels et al., 2015; Tickell et al., 2019; Access to Medicine Foundation, 2018.

claims.claim: Substandard or counterfeit drugs may not only be the inappropriate choice for the illness but may have suboptimal concentrations of antimicrobial, favouring resistance, and can potentially be toxic to the patients.
claims.source: Such medicines may not only be the inappropriate choice for the illness but may have suboptimal concentrations of antimicrobial, favouring resistance, and can potentially be toxic to the patients (Kelesidis and Falagas, 2015; Pisani, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kelesidis and Falagas, 2015 and Pisani, 2015.

claims.claim: In the case of TB, which requires prolonged multidrug therapy, one consequence of drug shortages will be short-term treatment interruptions potentially leading to increased risk of treatment failure and development of resistance.
claims.source: In the case of TB, which requires prolonged multidrug therapy, one consequence of drug shortages will be short-term treatment interruptions potentially leading to increased risk of treatment failure and development of resistance (Adepoju, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adepoju, 2020.

claims.claim: A reduction in income has been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Scotland.
claims.source: In high-income country (HIC) settings, where prescriptions for antibiotics are required, it is likely that a reduction in income will be associated with poorer health; such reductions have previously been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Scotland (Covvey et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Covvey et al., 2014.

claims.claim: A reduction in income has been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Sweden.
claims.source: such reductions have previously been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Scotland (Covvey et al., 2014), Sweden (Nilsson and Laurell, 2005)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nilsson and Laurell, 2005.

claims.claim: A reduction in income has been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in the US.
claims.source: such reductions have previously been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Scotland (Covvey et al., 2014), Sweden (Nilsson and Laurell, 2005), and, more recently, in the US (Kissler et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kissler et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Less prosperous socioeconomic areas within countries have experienced a higher burden of COVID-19.
claims.source: Similarly, less prosperous socioeconomic areas within such countries have experienced a higher burden of COVID-19 (Ahmed et al., 2020; Office for National Statistics, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2020 and Office for National Statistics, 2020.

claims.claim: Financial shocks due to COVID-19 policies may increase the need for people to use over-the-counter services including for unregulated antimicrobials in an attempt to reduce healthcare expenditure in LMIC settings.
claims.source: In LMIC settings, where there is already less regulation of antimicrobial purchasing, the financial shocks due to COVID-19 policies may increase the need for people to use over-the-counter services including for unregulated antimicrobials in an attempt to reduce healthcare expenditure (Frost et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Frost et al., 2019 and involves speculation about future behavior.

claims.claim: Subtherapeutic doses of drugs and shortened courses of antimicrobials have been associated with increased mortality.
claims.source: This presents a higher risk of subtherapeutic doses of drugs and shortened courses of antimicrobials, as well as increased mortality (Laxminarayan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laxminarayan et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Health systems that already struggle to provide sufficient access to antimicrobials may face further challenges to deliver due to the economic reverberations of the COVID-19 crisis.
claims.source: On the other hand, the economic reverberations of this crisis mean that health systems that already struggle to provide sufficient access to antimicrobials (Frost et al., 2019; Laxminarayan et al., 2016) may face further challenges to deliver
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frost et al., 2019 and Laxminarayan et al., 2016, and involves inference about future impacts.

claims.claim: Access to medicines has been shown to correlate with higher burden of preventable infections such as community-acquired pneumonia in children under 5.
claims.source: This may result in a potential increase in mortality, while such access has been shown to correlate with higher burden of preventable infections such as community-acquired pneumonia in children under 5 (Laxminarayan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laxminarayan et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Gender inequalities impact both COVID-19 and AMR due to the uneven distribution of infectious disease prevalence and burden.
claims.source: For example, gender inequalities impact both COVID-19 and AMR due to the uneven distribution of infectious disease prevalence and burden (Horton et al., 2016; McQuaid et al., 2020; Schröder et al., 2016; Wenham et al., 2020; Zanichelli et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horton et al., 2016; McQuaid et al., 2020; Schröder et al., 2016; Wenham et al., 2020; Zanichelli et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Black, Asian, and minority ethnic (BAME) populations suffer from both a greater economic impact and worse health outcomes from COVID-19.
claims.source: The pandemic has also highlighted racial inequality; in particular, the Black, Asian, and minority ethnic (BAME) categorisation has been used in some countries (Hu, 2020) to show how these populations suffer from both a greater economic impact and worse health outcomes from COVID-19 (Public Health England, 2020a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hu, 2020 and Public Health England, 2020a.

claims.claim: In the UK, BAME populations have higher rates of circulating AMR in the community.
claims.source: Emerging evidence suggests that in the UK BAME populations also have higher rates of circulating AMR in the community (Lishman et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lishman et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Countries with the greatest AMR burden are those in which spread of pathogens, rather than overuse of antimicrobials, is the dominant factor.
claims.source: It has been postulated that countries with the greatest AMR burden are those in which spread of pathogens, rather than overuse of antimicrobials, is the dominant factor (Collignon et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Collignon et al., 2018.

claims.claim: For MDR-TB, the majority of cases result from transmission events rather than acquisition of spontaneous resistance emerging during treatment.
claims.source: For MDR-TB – the largest single disease component of the global AMR burden (The Review on Antimicrobial Resistance, 2016) – the majority of cases result from transmission events rather than acquisition of spontaneous resistance emerging during treatment (Kendall et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to The Review on Antimicrobial Resistance, 2016 and Kendall et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Patients with severe COVID-19 may be hospitalised for prolonged periods of time.
claims.source: Patients with severe COVID-19 may be hospitalised for prolonged periods of time (Rees et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rees et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Patients hospitalised for prolonged periods of time are at high risk for acquiring nosocomial infections.
claims.source: Patients with severe COVID-19 may be hospitalised for prolonged periods of time (Rees et al., 2020), and hence are at high risk for acquiring nosocomial infections (Asensio et al., 1996; Oztoprak et al., 2006; Wolkewitz et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Asensio et al., 1996; Oztoprak et al., 2006; Wolkewitz et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Early anecdotal evidence from two acute care facilities in New York and Missouri reported three- to fourfold increases in central line-associated bloodstream infection rates, likely related to a shift towards a higher risk case-mix.
claims.source: Early anecdotal evidence from two acute care facilities in New York and Missouri reported three- to fourfold increases in central line-associated bloodstream infection rates, likely related to a shift towards a higher risk case-mix (McMullen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McMullen et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The hardships and resource strains due to COVID-19 have affected antimicrobial stewardship activities.
claims.source: The hardships and resource strains due to COVID-19 have also affected antimicrobial stewardship activities (Hsu, 2020; De Waele et al., 2021; Ginsburg and Klugman, 2020; Lynch et al., 2020; Seaton, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hsu, 2020; De Waele et al., 2021; Ginsburg and Klugman, 2020; Lynch et al., 2020; Seaton, 2020.

claims.claim: Antimicrobial stewardship programmes in hospitals have the potential to significantly reduce incidence of infections with ARO.
claims.source: It is known that antimicrobial stewardship programmes in hospitals have the potential to significantly reduce incidence of infections with ARO (Baur et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baur et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Increased acquisition of MRSA occurred during the SARS outbreak in 2003 in an intensive care unit in China.
claims.source: Some of these factors likely contributed to an increased acquisition of MRSA during the SARS outbreak in 2003 in an intensive care unit in China (Yap et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yap et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Handwashing alone could prevent 30% of diarrhoeal episodes in LMICs.
claims.source: Studies have shown that handwashing alone could prevent 30% of diarrhoeal episodes in LMICs (Ejemot-Nwadiaro et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ejemot-Nwadiaro et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Up to 50% of children with diarrhoea in LMICs receive antibiotics.
claims.source: As a result, increased hand hygiene to prevent SARS-CoV-2 transmission could reduce diarrhoeal incidence and hence the high number of antibiotic courses given to children with diarrhoea in LMICs (up to 50% with diarrhoea receive antibiotics) (Fink et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fink et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Low-level use of biocides can select for resistance both to the biocides and to antimicrobials.
claims.source: It has been shown that low-level use of these agents can select for resistance both to the biocides and to antimicrobials (Caselli, 2017; Hardy et al., 2018; Hora et al., 2020; Kampf, 2018; Maillard et al., 2020; McCarlie et al., 2020; Wales and Davies, 2015)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Caselli, 2017; Hardy et al., 2018; Hora et al., 2020; Kampf, 2018; Maillard et al., 2020; McCarlie et al., 2020; Wales and Davies, 2015.

claims.claim: Numbers of invasive bacterial infections appear to have decreased in 2020.
claims.source: For example, numbers of invasive bacterial infections appear to have decreased in 2020 (Brueggemann et al., 2020), such as Invasive Group A Streptococcal Infections in the UK (Public Health England, 2020a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brueggemann et al., 2020 and Public Health England, 2020a.

claims.claim: Many settings have seen far reduced influenza infection levels.
claims.source: Similarly, many settings have seen far reduced influenza infection levels (WHO, 2020n)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2020n.

claims.claim: Prolonged time at home due to COVID-19 interventions could result in increased transmission of other pathogens between household members.
claims.source: Within a household setting, prolonged time at home due to COVID-19 interventions could result in increased transmission of other pathogens between household members (Maillard et al., 2020) (e.g. of MRSA [Mollema et al., 2010], Streptococcus pneumoniae [Althouse et al., 2017], and MDR-TB [Grandjean et al., 2015; Leung et al., 2013; Paul and Kollikkara, 2014])
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maillard et al., 2020; Mollema et al., 2010; Althouse et al., 2017; Grandjean et al., 2015; Leung et al., 2013; Paul and Kollikkara, 2014.

claims.claim: MDR-TB usually only has 10% of transmission occurring within the home and is likely saturating.
claims.source: Alternatively, MDR-TB, a disease also caused by a respiratory pathogen, usually only has 10% of transmission occurring within the home and is likely saturating (Glynn et al., 2015; McCreesh and White, 2018; Middelkoop et al., 2015; Verver et al., 2004; Wilkinson et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Glynn et al., 2015; McCreesh and White, 2018; Middelkoop et al., 2015; Verver et al., 2004; Wilkinson et al., 1997.

claims.claim: Following travel to countries with high AMR prevalence, travellers can return colonised with bacteria carrying AMR genes and remain colonised for substantial periods of time.
claims.source: For example, it is known that following travel to countries with high AMR prevalence, travellers can return colonised with bacteria carrying AMR genes and remain colonised for substantial periods of time (Arcilla et al., 2017; ÖstholmBalkhed et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arcilla et al., 2017 and ÖstholmBalkhed et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Approximately three-quarters of programmes and service deliveries for HIV, TB, and malaria have been disrupted as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.
claims.source: Approximately three-quarters of programmes and service deliveries for HIV, TB, and malaria have been disrupted as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic (Fund, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fund, 2020.

claims.claim: South Africa and China have experienced large reductions in TB and MDR-TB testing in the first period of 2020.
claims.source: For example, South Africa and China have experienced large reductions in TB and MDR-TB testing in the first period of 2020 (Liu et al., 2020; National Institute for Communicable Diseases, Centre for Tuberculosis, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020 and National Institute for Communicable Diseases, Centre for Tuberculosis, 2020.

claims.claim: Successful treatment rates for patients with MDR-TB remain low at 56%.
claims.source: Successful treatment rates for patients with MDR-TB remain low at 56% (WHO, 2020g)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2020g.

claims.claim: Clinical care disruption may lead to a total reduction in in-patient antibiotic prescribing despite high levels of use in those with COVID-19.
claims.source: Clinical care disruption may lead to a total reduction in in-patient antibiotic prescribing despite high levels of use in those with COVID-19 (Clancy et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clancy et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Signs of a reduction in antibiotic use have been seen in healthcare settings in the US.
claims.source: Signs of a reduction in use have been seen in healthcare settings in the US, but a concomitantly larger reduction in bed days has sometimes led to an increased number of days of therapy per occupied bed day (Buehrle et al., 2020; Dieringer et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buehrle et al., 2020 and Dieringer et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Prescription of antibiotics to patients with COVID-19 clashes with the key public health message that antibiotics do not work for viral infections.
claims.source: The widely reported prescription of antibiotics to patients with COVID-19 clashes with the key public health message that antibiotics do not work for viral infections.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation about conflicting public health messages.

claims.claim: Following the 2009 influenza pandemic, patients in the community had greater expectations of receiving antibiotics for flu-like symptoms.
claims.source: This could lead to patients in the community having greater expectations of receiving antibiotics for flu-like symptoms, as was the case following the 2009 influenza pandemic (McNulty et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McNulty et al., 2012.

claims.claim: A potential signal of increased antibiotic prescribing has been seen in data from the UK.
claims.source: A potential signal of this has been seen in data from the UK (Armitage and Nellums, 2020; MacKenna, 2020) and likely increased prescribing for dental care (Croser, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Armitage and Nellums, 2020; MacKenna, 2020; and Croser, 2020.

claims.claim: In England there has been an up to 50% reduction in Accident and Emergency attendance in some regions.
claims.source: For example, in England there has been an up to 50% reduction in Accident and Emergency attendance in some regions (NHS England, 2020)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to NHS England, 2020.

claims.claim: In England there has been a 20% reduction in appointments.
claims.source: For example, in England there has been an up to 50% reduction in Accident and Emergency attendance in some regions (NHS England, 2020) and a 20% reduction in appointments (Armitage and Nellums, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Armitage and Nellums, 2020.

claims.claim: In the community in England, a reduction in prescriptions for some antibiotics has been seen, for example, for those used to treat skin and urinary tract infections (flucloxacillin and nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim).
claims.source: In the community in England, a reduction in prescriptions for some antibiotics has been seen, for example, for those used to treat skin and urinary tract infections (flucloxacillin and nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim) (MacKenna, 2020)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MacKenna, 2020.

claims.claim: Due to the decrease in the total number of appointments in England, the number of antibiotic prescriptions was higher than expected.
claims.source: but due to the decrease in the total number of appointments the number of antibiotic prescriptions was higher than expected (Armitage and Nellums, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Armitage and Nellums, 2020.

claims.claim: The fear of attending clinical settings, alongside the disruption to routine immunisation activities due to COVID-19-related burden, has led to reductions in overall vaccination coverage globally.
claims.source: The fear of attending clinical settings, alongside the disruption to routine immunisation activities due to COVID-19-related burden, has led to reductions in overall vaccination coverage globally (Bramer et al., 2020; McDonald et al., 2020; Saxena et al., 2020; WHO, 2020j).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bramer et al., 2020; McDonald et al., 2020; Saxena et al., 2020; WHO, 2020j.

claims.claim: Vaccines are a key tool to prevent infections, and hence antibiotic use and associated resistance.
claims.source: Vaccines are a key tool to prevent infections, and hence antibiotic use and associated resistance (Lipsitch and Siber, 2016; Malarski et al., 2019; ReAct, 2020; Sosler, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lipsitch and Siber, 2016; Malarski et al., 2019; ReAct, 2020; Sosler, 2020.

claims.claim: Some vaccines specifically target resistant subpopulations, for example, serotypes of S. pneumoniae with higher resistance to penicillin.
claims.source: Some vaccines also specifically target resistant subpopulations: for example, serotypes of S. pneumoniae with higher resistance to penicillin (Berger et al., 2019; Ginsburg and Klugman, 2017; Klugman and Black, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berger et al., 2019; Ginsburg and Klugman, 2017; Klugman and Black, 2018.

claims.claim: The world's cheapest and safest vaccine, Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG), had global availability and procurement issues from 2013 to 2019.
claims.source: Vaccines are also susceptible to supply issues: the world's cheapest and safest vaccine, Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG), had global availability and procurement issues from 2013 to 2019 (UNICEF, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to UNICEF, 2019.

claims.claim: BCG immunisation levels have already declined due to COVID-19 health system disruptions in India and Pakistan.
claims.source: BCG immunisation levels have already declined due to COVID-19 health system disruptions in India and Pakistan (Chandir, 2020; Rukmini, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chandir, 2020 and Rukmini, 2020.

claims.claim: An emphasis on avoiding a dual 'flu and COVID-19' health burden has led to increased coverage of influenza vaccination (e.g. in England).
claims.source: A positive consequence of COVID-19 has been an emphasis on avoiding a dual 'flu and COVID-19' health burden, leading to increased coverage of influenza vaccination (e.g. in England; Public Health England, 2020c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Public Health England, 2020c.

claims.claim: Increased influenza vaccination will have the knock-on effect of reducing antimicrobial prescribing, both inappropriate and appropriate, for influenza-like infections and secondary bacterial complications.
claims.source: This will have the knock-on effect of reducing antimicrobial prescribing, both inappropriate and appropriate, for influenza-like infections and secondary bacterial complications (Klein et al., 2020; Knight et al., 2018a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klein et al., 2020 and Knight et al., 2018a.

claims.claim: Compared to rapid programmes already started in HICs, many low-income countries will have few COVID-19 vaccine doses in 2021.
claims.source: However, vaccination programmes are slow and highly variable: compared to rapid programmes already started in HICs, many low-income countries will have few vaccines doses in 2021 (Dyer, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dyer, 2020.

claims.claim: The WHO has recently published measures to ensure that antimicrobial stewardship is integrated into pandemic responses.
claims.source: The WHO has recently published measures to ensure that antimicrobial stewardship is integrated into pandemic responses (Getahun et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Getahun et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Staff, equipment such as PCR machines for diagnostic laboratories, and reagents have been redeployed to COVID-19 research.
claims.source: Staff, equipment such as PCR machines for diagnostic laboratories (Cepheid, 2020; Department of Health and Social Care, 2020), and reagents have been redeployed to COVID-19 research.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cepheid, 2020 and Department of Health and Social Care, 2020.

claims.claim: Clinical trials for AMR have been put on hold due to COVID-19.
claims.source: The impact of this will not only be interruption to crucial research that would otherwise have been performed, such as clinical trials that have been put on hold (Cleary, 2020; Rusen, 2020; Thornton, 2020)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cleary, 2020; Rusen, 2020; Thornton, 2020.

claims.claim: Figure 1 highlights the variability across the intersection of COVID-19 and AMR and can be used to support the identification of research priorities.
claims.source: This is not exhaustive but highlights the variability across the intersection and can be used to support the identification of research priorities.
claims.evidence: This claim refers to Figure 1 and its purpose.

results.result: AMR was a top global public health priority before COVID-19, which was declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. AMR had been specifically named a priority for 2020.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 establish the contextual background of AMR as a pre-existing priority and the timing of the COVID-19 pandemic declaration. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to WHO documents and represent well-established facts.

results.result: AMR likely caused approximately 1.8 million deaths in 2020, about one-third as many as COVID-19, based on MDR-TB deaths (182,000 in 2019) representing one-third of the AMR burden.
results.evaluation: The calculation in C6 relies on extrapolation from MDR-TB data (C4) and the assumption that MDR-TB represents one-third of AMR burden (C5). While individual data points are cited, the inference chain involves substantial uncertainty and the comparison to COVID-19 deaths depends on timing and data quality. The mathematical logic appears sound but the underlying assumptions require validation.

results.result: COVID-19 symptoms resemble bacterial pneumonia and biomarkers like C-reactive protein may be elevated, leading to empiric antibiotic prescribing despite low secondary bacterial infection rates (<20%).
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 form a coherent narrative about diagnostic challenges and prescribing patterns in COVID-19. Each claim is supported by appropriate citations, and the logical connection between symptom overlap, diagnostic uncertainty, and prescribing behavior is well-established.

results.result: Inappropriate antimicrobial treatment increases mortality risk, and in high carbapenem-resistance areas, less safe antibiotics like colistin may be used as first-line therapy.
results.evaluation: Both claims are supported by appropriate citations. C11 establishes the general principle of treatment appropriateness, while C12 provides a specific example of how local resistance patterns influence prescribing decisions. The connection to COVID-19 care is implicit but logical.

results.result: AMR evolution is determined by emergence (driven by selective pressures leading to resistance acquisition through mutation or horizontal gene transfer), transmission (enabled or prevented by environmental conditions and behaviors), and population-level infection burden.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 establish a conceptual framework for understanding AMR evolution. The framework is well-cited and represents established knowledge in the field. This provides the theoretical foundation for analyzing COVID-19's impact on AMR.

results.result: Up to 70% of COVID-19 patients receive antimicrobials, and survivors may develop chronic lung disease with extensive damage, leading to increased risk of colonization with resistant organisms like P. aeruginosa.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C20 describe antimicrobial use in COVID-19 patients and potential long-term consequences. Each claim is supported by citations. The progression from acute treatment (C17) to potential chronic sequelae (C18-C19) to AMR risk (C20) is logical, though C18 and C20 involve some speculation about future outcomes.

results.result: Despite mounting evidence of lack of efficacy, chloroquine has been used for COVID-19, raising concerns about resistance in malaria settings where it remains the drug of choice. COVID-19 symptoms can be mistaken for malaria or TB, and bystander selection has been observed with azithromycin use in trachoma campaigns.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C24 describe the problematic use of antimalarials for COVID-19 and the risk of bystander selection. All claims are well-cited. The concern about chloroquine resistance in malaria is particularly relevant given symptom overlap (C23) and precedent from azithromycin (C24).

results.result: Use of hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and azithromycin for COVID-19 has been halted in some settings like the US, but continued in many African countries and India despite WHO recommendations.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 document geographic variation in COVID-19 treatment practices. All claims are supported by citations. The contrast between evidence-based discontinuation in some settings and continued use in others highlights important disparities in pandemic response.

results.result: Cheap, rapid tests may detect SARS-CoV-2 earlier and prevent antibiotic use, but current diagnostics like lateral flow tests remain insensitive and risk false negatives.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 present both the potential and limitations of rapid diagnostics. Both claims are cited, though C28 involves inference about impact on antibiotic use. The tension between diagnostic potential and current limitations is clearly articulated.

results.result: Prolonged changes in antimicrobial use during COVID-19 could increase antimicrobial production and environmental concentrations, affecting selective pressures for AMR in water and soil systems.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 involves speculation about environmental impacts of increased antimicrobial use. While cited, the claim is explicitly conditional ('if prolonged') and involves multiple inferential steps from human use to environmental concentrations to AMR selection. The mechanism is plausible but lacks direct evidence.

results.result: Antibiotic supply chains are fragile, as demonstrated by a single Chinese factory disruption causing international piperacillin-tazobactam shortages. Most countries import antibiotics (80-90% of generics in the UK), and COVID-19 has led to reduced exports from manufacturing countries like India and azithromycin shortages.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 document supply chain vulnerabilities and COVID-19 impacts. All claims are well-cited with specific examples and data. The progression from pre-existing fragility (C31) to import dependence (C32-C33) to COVID-19 disruptions (C34-C35) is logical and evidence-based.

results.result: LMICs are particularly vulnerable to supply chain issues due to weak health systems and poor quality control. Uneven antimicrobial supplies raise AMR concerns, and substandard/counterfeit drugs may have suboptimal concentrations favoring resistance. For TB, drug shortages lead to treatment interruptions risking resistance development.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 describe supply chain vulnerabilities in LMICs and consequences for AMR. All claims are well-cited. The progression from general vulnerability (C36) to specific concerns about drug quality (C37-C38) to disease-specific impacts (C39) is logical and evidence-based.

results.result: Income reduction has been associated with higher rates of respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Scotland, Sweden, and the US. Less prosperous socioeconomic areas have experienced higher COVID-19 burden.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 document the relationship between socioeconomic factors, health outcomes, and antibiotic use across multiple countries. All claims are well-cited. The evidence from multiple settings strengthens the generalizability of the finding.

results.result: Financial shocks from COVID-19 may increase unregulated antimicrobial use in LMICs to reduce healthcare costs, presenting risks of subtherapeutic dosing and increased mortality. Health systems may face challenges delivering antimicrobial access, potentially increasing mortality from preventable infections like pneumonia in children under 5.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 describe economic impacts on antimicrobial access and use in LMICs. All claims are cited, though C44 and C46 involve speculation about future impacts. The tension between inappropriate overuse and inadequate access is well-articulated, representing a key challenge in LMIC settings.

results.result: Gender and racial inequalities impact both COVID-19 and AMR. BAME populations suffer greater economic impact and worse COVID-19 outcomes, and in the UK have higher rates of circulating AMR in the community.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 document health inequalities affecting both COVID-19 and AMR. All claims are well-cited. The intersection of multiple forms of inequality (gender, race) with both health challenges represents an important syndemic perspective.

results.result: Countries with the greatest AMR burden are those where pathogen spread dominates over antimicrobial overuse. For MDR-TB, the majority of cases result from transmission rather than treatment-emergent resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 establish the importance of transmission in AMR epidemiology. Both claims are well-cited. This provides important context for understanding how COVID-19 infection prevention measures might impact AMR, particularly for MDR-TB.

results.result: Severe COVID-19 patients may be hospitalized for prolonged periods at high risk for nosocomial infections. Early evidence shows 3-4 fold increases in central line-associated bloodstream infections. COVID-19 has affected antimicrobial stewardship activities, though such programs can significantly reduce ARO infections. Increased MRSA acquisition occurred during the 2003 SARS outbreak.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 describe healthcare-associated infection risks during COVID-19. All claims are well-cited. The historical precedent from SARS (C58) strengthens the plausibility of similar impacts from COVID-19. The tension between increased infection risk and disrupted stewardship is clearly articulated.

results.result: Handwashing could prevent 30% of diarrheal episodes in LMICs, where up to 50% of children with diarrhea receive antibiotics. However, low-level biocide use can select for resistance to both biocides and antimicrobials.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 describe the dual effects of increased hygiene measures. All claims are well-cited. The potential benefit of reduced diarrheal disease and antibiotic use (C60-C61) is balanced against concerns about biocide resistance (C62).

results.result: Numbers of invasive bacterial infections and influenza infection levels appear to have decreased in 2020.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 document reductions in other infections during COVID-19. Both claims are cited with data. These findings suggest that COVID-19 prevention measures may have broader benefits for infection control, though reporting issues may also contribute.

results.result: Prolonged time at home could increase household transmission of pathogens including MRSA, S. pneumoniae, and MDR-TB. However, MDR-TB transmission is usually only 10% within homes and may be saturating.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 present contrasting perspectives on household transmission. Both are well-cited. C66 provides an important counterpoint to C65, suggesting that for some pathogens like MDR-TB, increased household time may not substantially increase transmission.

results.result: Following travel to high AMR prevalence countries, travelers can return colonized with bacteria carrying AMR genes and remain colonized for substantial periods.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 establishes the role of international travel in AMR spread. The claim is well-cited. This provides context for understanding how COVID-19 travel restrictions might impact AMR transmission patterns.

results.result: Approximately three-quarters of HIV, TB, and malaria programs have been disrupted by COVID-19. South Africa and China experienced large reductions in TB/MDR-TB testing in early 2020. MDR-TB treatment success rates remain low at 56%.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 document COVID-19's impact on other disease programs. All claims are well-cited with specific data. The combination of widespread disruption (C68), specific testing reductions (C69), and already-low success rates (C70) highlights serious concerns for TB control.

results.result: Clinical care disruption may reduce total inpatient antibiotic prescribing despite high use in COVID-19 patients. US healthcare settings show reduced antibiotic use but increased days of therapy per occupied bed day.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 describe complex changes in antibiotic use patterns. Both claims are cited. The finding that reduced overall use may mask increased intensity of use per patient (C72) represents an important nuance in understanding COVID-19's impact on antimicrobial consumption.

results.result: Antibiotic prescription for COVID-19 clashes with public health messaging that antibiotics don't work for viral infections. Following the 2009 influenza pandemic, patients had greater expectations of receiving antibiotics for flu-like symptoms. Signals of increased antibiotic prescribing have been seen in UK data.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 describe public health messaging challenges and behavioral impacts. C73 is a logical observation, C74 is cited historical precedent, and C75 is cited data. The progression from messaging conflict to historical precedent to current signals is logical and concerning.

results.result: England experienced up to 50% reduction in A&E attendance and 20% reduction in appointments. Community prescriptions for some antibiotics decreased, but antibiotic prescriptions per appointment were higher than expected.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 document changes in healthcare utilization and prescribing in England. All claims are well-cited with specific data. The finding that reduced overall prescribing masks increased prescribing intensity (C79) parallels findings from US hospitals (C72).

results.result: Fear of clinical settings and COVID-19 disruptions have reduced global vaccination coverage. Vaccines prevent infections and thus antibiotic use and resistance. Some vaccines specifically target resistant subpopulations like penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae serotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 describe vaccination disruptions and the role of vaccines in AMR control. All claims are well-cited. The connection between vaccination, infection prevention, and AMR is well-established, making disruptions particularly concerning.

results.result: BCG vaccine had global availability issues from 2013-2019. BCG immunization levels have declined due to COVID-19 health system disruptions in India and Pakistan.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 document BCG vaccine supply and coverage issues. Both claims are well-cited. The combination of pre-existing supply problems (C83) and COVID-19 disruptions (C84) raises serious concerns for TB prevention.

results.result: Emphasis on avoiding dual flu and COVID-19 burden has increased influenza vaccination coverage in England. This will reduce antimicrobial prescribing for influenza-like infections and secondary bacterial complications.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 describe a positive consequence of COVID-19 for vaccination. C85 is cited data, while C86 involves inference about downstream effects. The inference is logical and supported by citations, representing a beneficial side effect of pandemic response.

results.result: Compared to rapid programs in HICs, many low-income countries will have few COVID-19 vaccine doses in 2021.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 documents vaccine inequity. The claim is cited and represents a well-documented concern about global vaccine distribution. This has implications for the duration of pandemic impacts on AMR in different settings.

results.result: WHO has published measures to ensure antimicrobial stewardship is integrated into pandemic responses.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 documents WHO guidance. The claim is appropriately cited. This represents an important policy response to the intersection of COVID-19 and AMR.

results.result: Staff, equipment, and reagents have been redeployed to COVID-19 research. AMR clinical trials have been put on hold. Routine microbiology samples for global AMR monitoring systems like GLASS will be missing for 2020.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 document COVID-19's impact on AMR research and surveillance. All claims are well-cited. The disruption to both research (C89-C90) and surveillance (C91) has serious implications for AMR knowledge and response capacity.

results.result: Companies developing novel antimicrobials were already susceptible to failure. The US has developed legislation for antibiotic funding mechanisms (PASTEUR Act), and the UK has developed a scheme to pay pharmaceutical companies upfront for antimicrobial development.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe the antimicrobial development pipeline and policy responses. All claims are well-cited. The progression from market failure (C92) to policy interventions (C93-C94) represents important efforts to address antimicrobial development challenges.

results.result: SARS-CoV-2 highlights how difficult an untreatable ARO would be to control once it has emerged.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 draws an analogy between COVID-19 and potential ARO emergence. The claim is cited and involves inference. The analogy is logical and provides important perspective on AMR risks, though the comparison has limitations (e.g., transmission routes, population immunity).

results.result: A WHO report found no clear evidence that National Action Plans for Health Security relate to a country's ability to respond to COVID-19.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 reports findings from a WHO assessment. The claim is appropriately cited. This finding has concerning implications for AMR National Action Plans if similar patterns hold.

results.result: Vietnam has low COVID-19 cases (1,539 as of Jan 2021) but 3,234 confirmed MDR-TB cases in 2019. Greece has relatively low COVID-19 deaths (5,488 as of Jan 2021) but ~40% of infections in 2018 were antibiotic-resistant, with the highest EU/EEA incidence of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 provide country-specific examples of varying COVID-19 and AMR burdens. All claims are well-cited with specific data. These examples illustrate the importance of context-specific prioritization and the risk that COVID-19 response may overshadow more pressing AMR concerns in some settings.

results.result: India had more than 10.5 million confirmed COVID-19 cases in January 2021 and has one of the largest numbers of AMR infections globally.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 document India's dual burden of COVID-19 and AMR. Both claims are well-cited. India represents a critical case where both challenges are severe, with high potential for mutual exacerbation.

results.result: Across the world, inequalities are rising between and within countries.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 describes global inequality trends. The claim is cited. This provides important context for understanding how COVID-19 and AMR impacts may be distributed unequally.

results.result: Figure 1 highlights the variability across the intersection of COVID-19 and AMR and can be used to support identification of research priorities.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 describes the purpose of Figure 1. The figure provides a comprehensive visual framework organizing the multiple dimensions of COVID-19's impact on AMR emergence, transmission, and burden. The claim accurately represents the figure's content and utility.
